You are a blind semantic decoder of a natural-language crystal description. The user message is your only source of material-specific information. Understand the spatial narrative and produce a construction plan; do not guess missing independent numbers or look up a material. Return one JSON object only, without Markdown fences.
For sufficient information use:
{"status":"ok","space_group_number":integer,"hall_symbol":"Hall symbol stated in the text","lattice":[input_a,input_b,input_c,input_alpha,input_beta,input_gamma],"composition":{"Element":input_cell_atom_count},"orbits":[{"element":"Element","wyckoff":"multiplicity_and_letter","representative":[standard_fractional_x,standard_fractional_y,standard_fractional_z]}],"frame_transform":{"matrix":[[p11,p12,p13],[p21,p22,p23],[p31,p32,p33]],"origin_shift":[s1,s2,s3]},"round_digits":integer_or_null,"precision_corrections":[{"element":"Element","at":[input_fractional_x_before_correction,input_fractional_y_before_correction,input_fractional_z_before_correction],"delta":[fractional_dx,fractional_dy,fractional_dz]}]}
Lengths use angstroms, angles use degrees. The specified lattice and composition refer to the original input cell. Orbit representatives refer to the standard Hall coordinate frame. Copy the Hall symbol as a mathematical identifier rather than guessing a public-table integer number. Any equivalent representative of a declared orbit is allowed. Distinct independent orbits of the same element remain separate.
The geometry engine expands the public Hall symmetry orbits, applies q_input = inverse(P)(q_standard - s), selects images in the input cell, rounds fractional coordinates if round_digits is given, and applies precision corrections at their identified input-frame atom positions. If the text explicitly uses identical frames, supply identity P and zero shift. If no rounding is specified, use null. If no corrections are specified, use an empty array. All sites have full occupancy.
Numerical relations in the prose should be resolved into numbers in the plan. Do not silently replace the original geometry with an idealized one. For missing required information return {"status":"insufficient_information","reason":"..."}; for contradictory constraints return {"status":"conflict","reason":"..."}. Your input contains no source CIF or hidden data. Public crystallographic definitions are allowed; material-specific external retrieval is not.

The crystal is described in a tetragonal unit cell with lattice parameters a = b = 3.591363 Å and c = 4.410464 Å, all interaxial angles being exactly 90 degrees. The input cell contains six atoms in total, corresponding to the composition Li₂H₂O₂, and the structure adopts the tetragonal space group P4/nmm (space-group number 129, Hall symbol "-P 4a 2a"). All atomic positions are reported as fractional coordinates, and the standard crystallographic frame is related to the input frame by q_standard = P q_input + s. In this case the transformation matrix P is essentially the identity matrix, with only negligible numerical noise on the order of 10⁻³³ to 10⁻³⁴ in the off-diagonal terms, while the origin shift s is exactly (1/4, 3/4, 0). This means the input cell is already aligned with the conventional tetragonal axes, but its origin is displaced by one quarter of the a axis and three quarters of the b axis relative to the standard setting.

Within this cell, the lithium atoms occupy the Wyckoff orbit 2a. The representative lithium position in the standard frame is (3/4, 1/4, 0), and the symmetry of P4/nmm generates a second equivalent lithium atom, giving two lithium atoms per cell. These lithium sites lie on the basal plane z = 0 and are related by the fourfold and mirror operations of the space group.

Hydrogen occupies the Wyckoff orbit 2c, with representative coordinates (1/4, 1/4, z), where the independent height parameter is z = 0.412974 (rounded to six decimal places). The symmetry operations produce a second hydrogen atom at the symmetry-related position generated from this representative, so that the two hydrogen atoms form a pair displaced along the c axis above and below the reference plane at the same in-plane position (1/4, 1/4).

Oxygen also occupies a 2c orbit, distinct from that of hydrogen, with representative coordinates (1/4, 1/4, z) but with its own independent height z = 0.193022. Again, the space-group symmetry generates the second oxygen atom, yielding two oxygen atoms per unit cell. Thus both hydrogen and oxygen lie on the same in-plane line at x = y = 1/4, but at different heights along c: oxygen at z ≈ 0.193 and hydrogen at z ≈ 0.413, with their symmetry partners completing the 2c multiplicities.

No precision corrections beyond the stated six-decimal rounding are required for any of the atomic positions; all listed fractional coordinates already represent the input geometry consistently within the declared P4/nmm symmetry.
